facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Leverage moved in two steps. Reported total debt to EBITDA was 1.82x in FY2024, rose to 6.28x in FY2025 and stands at 3.71x on a trailing-twelve-month basis at Q3 2026, with net leverage of 3.35x, or 3.42x pro forma for the USD 10.2 million dividend payable on 2026-12-01. The Phoenix Global purchase was funded with cash and revolver borrowing, taking carrying debt from USD 492.3 million to USD 685.5 million, and the USD 90.3 million Haverhill I impairment pulled FY2025 reported EBITDA down to USD 109.2 million. The trailing window at Q3 2026 still contains the negative Q4 2025 reported EBITDA of USD 39.0 million, so reported leverage will fall when that quarter leaves the window, provided Q4 2026 reported EBITDA is above that negative level. facts.text: Cash-flow quality is improving but depends on receivables. facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: The earnings improvement is acquisition-led. Nine-month adjusted EBITDA rose USD 40.5 million to USD 203.0 million, but Industrial Services contributed a rise of USD 53.1 million, from seven more months of Phoenix Global, while Domestic Coke fell USD 5.5 million as lower volumes after the Haverhill I shutdown and weaker energy results more than offset better pricing and yields. Cliffs Steel supplied 61.7% of nine-month revenue, so the cash flows behind take-or-pay contracts depend heavily on one counterparty group. One support is contracted volume: coke sales agreements carry 16.2 million tons of unsatisfied obligations and Industrial Services holds USD 505.8 million of fixed-fee and take-or-pay revenue. rows.label: Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- High: No executed credit agreement, indenture, guarantee or collateral document and no guarantor list were supplied, and the relative legal rank of the revolver and the notes is not stated. The debt stack therefore shows only the notes, and covenant headroom, structural priority and recovery cannot be established. The agreements and the guarantor exhibit would close this. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18 - Medium: Reported EBITDA is constructed because the issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, and the add-backs behind the issuer-adjusted figure are not component-tested or assessed for realisation. Leverage on either basis is therefore indicative, and covenant EBITDA is not established. The issuer's definition schedule and debt agreement would close this. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation C12 - Medium: Q1 2025 interest paid is a dash, so trailing cash interest and EBITDA coverage at the first quarter of 2026 are not calculable. A cash flow statement printing the figure would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 10 - Medium: Receivables rose sharply in 2026 and the issuer attributes the rise to timing of customer payments without quantifying it, so the quality of the nine-month operating cash flow is not fully established. An ageing and customer-level payment schedule would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C11 - Low: Source dashes and lines not printed in a statement are shown as not supplied, not zero, in the income statement, cash flow and balance sheet tables, for example debt issuance costs before Q3 2025, the FX effect on cash and interest payable. Reported totals remain usable; fuller statements would close these cells. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 92–93; 10-Q_2026-03-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-Q_2026-06-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-K_2024-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 91–92; 10-Q_2026-03-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; 10-Q_2026-06-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9 - Low: The 2023 balance sheet prints goodwill within intangible assets and revolver availability at 2023-12-31 is not stated. Leverage and net debt for FY2023 are supported; the liquidity row for that date states cash only. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-K_2024-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 74 - Low: The Algoma Steel settlement reached in October 2026 has no stated amount, date or accounting, and the pro forma effect is not established. The settlement agreement or a later filing would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26 - Low: Gross profit, maintenance capital expenditure, restricted cash and a standardised FFO measure are not printed, so they are not established; no value is assumed. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 35–36

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Cash flow is contract-anchored but concentrated in two customer groups. Take-or-pay terms oblige customers to buy the contracted tons or pay the contract price, and coal cost passes through when targeted yields are met, so volume risk and most coal-price risk sit with the customers, while yield shortfalls and operating-cost overruns stay with SunCoke. Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel together supplied 75.8% of FY2025 revenue and owed 36% of the receivables balance at year-end, so the credit is in practice an exposure to the solvency and renewal decisions of those two groups. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 104–105; calculation C02

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The contract calendar is the nearest business risk. The Granite City agreement with U.S. Steel was extended only to 2026-12-31, which is 43 days after the analysis date, the Algoma Steel volume at Haverhill II ends in December 2026 and is already in dispute, while the Cliffs Steel agreements run to 2028, 2032 and 2035 and the ArcelorMittal Brazil operating agreement to January 2028. A lapse or weaker repricing at Granite City would push volume at that plant into non-contracted sales, which are priced at spot and export market levels and carry none of the take-or-pay protection. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–13; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73; calculation C06

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a benign owner-behaviour reading is the combination of a debt-funded acquisition and a dividend paid through a weak free cash flow year: in FY2025 dividends and minority distributions of USD 48.8 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 42.3 million, and carrying debt rose after the Phoenix Global purchase. The view would change to a higher governance risk if the credit agreement or indenture shows wide restricted-payment, investment or asset-transfer capacity, if the proxy statement discloses a large holder or related-party arrangements, or if the board sustains the dividend while leverage stays high. It would change toward lower business risk if the Granite City agreement is renewed on similar economics for a multi-year term, and if the Algoma Steel settlement delivers cash or replacement contracts. facts.label: T2D.9 Sponsor and governance risk assessment
facts.text: Overall, SunCoke presents medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behaviour is a debt-funded acquisition followed by revolver repayment while the dividend continued, which matters because it raised and then lowered leverage without sponsor involvement and implies creditors rely on operating cash flow, not an equity owner. Countervailing evidence is the suspended repurchase programme and the absence of any priming or exchange transaction in the filings read. Further analysis requires the debt agreements and the proxy statement. The governance review is completed with limitations. tables.limitation: Sponsor and governance risk level: Medium. Basis: Source readiness (CP-0) Overall, SunCoke presents medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behaviour is a debt-funded acquisition followed by revolver repayment while the dividend continued, which matters because it raised and then lowered leverage without sponsor involvement and implies creditors rely on operating cash flow, not an equity owner. Countervailing evidence is the suspended repurchase programme and the absence of any priming or exchange transaction in the filings read. Further analysis requires the debt agreements and the proxy statement. The governance review is completed with limitations. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The contract calendar links business risk to refinancing risk. The Granite City agreement with U.S. Steel ends on 2026-12-31, 43 days after the analysis date, and covers 20.6% of contracted tons; the Haverhill II agreement, at 17.5%, ends in December 2028, so 38.1% of contracted tons comes up for renegotiation by the end of 2028, ahead of the 2029 notes. FY2025 results already cite the economics of the Granite City extension as a drag, and the January 2026 extension was again only one year on similar terms, so repricing is a demonstrated risk, not a hypothetical one. facts.label: Ownership, group structure and financial policy
facts.text: Behaviour since 2020 has been to suspend repurchases (USD 96.3 million of the authorisation is unused), to keep a quarterly dividend of USD 0.12 per share, to fund the USD 294.0 million Phoenix Global purchase with cash and revolver, and then to repay USD 86.0 million of that revolver in nine months. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue in the contracted core is predictable, but the contract label overstates how fixed it is. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next two years the tailwinds are mechanical and operational: trailing reported leverage falls when the negative Q4 2025 reported EBITDA of USD 39.0 million leaves the window, provided Q4 2026 reported EBITDA is above that level; favourable coal-to-coke yields lifted Domestic Coke adjusted EBITDA per ton to USD 58.40 in Q3 2026 against USD 46.27 a year earlier; terminals volumes are rising; and repayment of the revolver lowers floating-rate interest. These support leverage reduction and refinancing confidence. The headwinds are the Granite City decision by 2026-12-31, the Haverhill I volume loss (Domestic Coke sales volumes were 8.0% lower in Q3), receivables that must convert, an Algoma recovery that is unknown, and a property insurance recovery of USD 6.9 million, relating to a 2023 flood event, that inflates Q3 reported EBITDA and is one-off by nature. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The issuer-specific downside is a second Algoma-type event at the nearest renewal, joined to a receivable balance that does not convert. The initiating condition is that U.S. Steel does not renew Granite City after 2026-12-31 on similar terms. The first operational break is that the plant's take-or-pay volume, 20.6% of contracted tons, would be sold at spot and export prices without pass-through protection, or idled, lifting indicative non-contracted capacity from 22.5% to 38.5% of nameplate. The financial transmission follows at the average Domestic Coke earnings of USD 49.67 per ton: about USD 29.3 million of adjusted EBITDA, 11.3% of the trailing figure, would be at risk. Leverage on that illustration would move from 2.09x to 2.36x on adjusted EBITDA and from 3.35x (3.42x pro forma for the dividend payable on 2026-12-01) to 4.09x on reported EBITDA, and interest cover would fall from 7.04x to 6.24x and from 4.39x to 3.60x; the covenant definitions are not supplied, so headroom against the 4.50x and 2.50x levels is not established. The first observable sign would be Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 Domestic Coke volumes, with the quarterly report for Q1 2027 the first to show a full quarter without the contract. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, SunCoke presents an adequate business profile supported by take-or-pay contracts with cost pass-through, heat-recovery technology and a distant maturity profile, but credit quality is constrained by two-customer concentration, a contract calendar that starts to expire on 2026-12-31 and an unconverted receivable build. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because trailing free cash flow of USD 119.3 million covers payouts 2.45x and adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest 7.04x, although both rest on receivables converting and on customers performing. Against typical leveraged-credit issuers serving the steel industry, whose volumes are usually priced at market, the contracted structure is a differentiator, but no peer data were supplied, so the comparison is qualitative, and the financial profile trend is improving. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewal terms for Granite City and Haverhill II, on the value of the contracted earnings in 2028, and on market access that the filings do not evidence beyond a debt fair value of 95.7% of principal. The primary downside path is a customer non-renewal or refusal combined with slow collections, which would lift leverage and draw the revolver. Further analysis would require the debt agreements and guarantor list, receivable ageing, plant-level margins, the Algoma settlement terms and current market pricing. Fundamental credit analysis completed. Top risk: customer concentration and recontracting at the two steel customers. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C13

tables.limitation: The five filings cover one reporting entity, SunCoke Energy, Inc., consolidated with its subsidiaries; there is no parent group, and the only third-party equity in the perimeter is the 14.8% interest in the Indiana Harbor cokemaking facility. Audited FY2024 and FY2025 statements and unaudited statements through 2026-09-30 are present, as are the debt, lease, benefit, customer and contract notes, so the gate is met with limitations: no executed debt agreement, guarantor list, proxy statement or market data was supplied, and nothing dated after the third-quarter report of 2026-10-27 was available. Module status is ready with limitations. Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 39 Each datapoint taken from the earlier analyses was re-derived from the filings before use, as the table restates. One earlier statement is corrected here. The business and governance analysis lists the issue date and terms of the 2029 notes as not found, but the exhibit index of the 2025 annual report dates the indenture 2021-06-22 and names subsidiary guarantors as parties to it; the guarantor names and the indenture terms remain unsupplied. Debt fair value, reclamation surety bonds, coal purchase commitments and scheduled interest are additions to the earlier analyses, not changes to them. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 137

tables.title: Business and company description — Facility

columns.label: Contract volume, thousand tons a year

tables.limitation: SunCoke is the largest independent producer of coke in the Americas by tons produced, with about 38% of U.S. blast furnace coke capacity in five U.S. cokemaking plants whose capacity and contracts are set out in the table below, plus a sixth plant in Brazil that it operates for ArcelorMittal Brazil for fees. Most coke is sold to Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel under long-term take-or-pay agreements; unreserved capacity is sold as foundry coke and into spot and export markets. Since the August 2025 acquisition of Phoenix Global the group also provides mill services and slag handling at about fifteen steel-plant sites in four countries alongside its bulk-material terminals, and these Industrial Services produced 19.4% of nine-month 2026 revenue against 4.2% in FY2024. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation C08 The model supports debt service because customers pay fixed fees and most input costs while they perform, which gives revenue visibility of about eight years on a weighted basis; it weakens refinancing confidence because the same contracts rest on two counterparties and expire in clusters in 2026, 2028, 2032 and 2035. Contracted volume is concentrated in Cliffs Steel and falls due on different dates, as the table shows; shares are the module's calculation on the volumes stated or, for Middletown and Indiana Harbor, on full nameplate capacity. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C10

tables.title: Financial profile and credit quality — Instrument
tables.limitation: The nine dimensions of the financial profile come out mostly average, with diversification the weak point. Scale and market position are average: SunCoke is the largest independent coke producer in the Americas, but its trailing revenue of USD 1,896.5 million is small beside its customers. Competitive advantage is average: heat-recovery technology and long contracts are real, but a customer has breached and Granite City renews a year at a time. Business diversification is weak: two customers supply 75.7% of revenue and the new Industrial Services business serves the same steel end market. Cost and capex flexibility is average: costs largely pass through but ongoing capital spending is required. Margin stability is average: adjusted margin was 14.10% in FY2024, 11.93% in FY2025 and 13.69% trailing. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation C09; calculation C15 Free cash flow stability is average and improving: free cash flow ranged from USD 42.3 million in FY2025 to USD 139.8 million in FY2023, and is USD 119.3 million trailing, with receivables unresolved. Ability to refinance is average: nothing matures before 2029, management's fair value estimate of debt is 95.7% of principal, and the two ratings of BB- and B1 were reaffirmed in mid-2025, before the Haverhill I impairment; the cover page also values non-affiliate equity at USD 721.1 million at 2025-06-30, a stale figure. Liquidity position is average: USD 275.6 million, mostly undrawn revolver. Financial policy and governance is average: dividends were held through a debt-funded acquisition and then revolver debt was repaid, but legal capacity and board detail are not supplied. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation C01; calculation C04; calculation C13 The table sets out all borrowed debt at 2026-09-30, because the covenant and priority questions turn on its terms. The next table sets out claims outside the borrowed-debt figure and says for each whether it is inside it. The third table computes liquidity from printed inputs, by facility. Credit supports are the contract core, the distant maturities and the cash-funded repayment; constraints are concentration, the receivable build and the unseen debt terms. The trend is improving: net debt is down USD 53.6 million since year-end and trailing adjusted leverage is 2.09x against 2.72x at FY2025, with no adjusted-basis pro forma for the dividend payable on 2026-12-01 established. Claims outside borrowed debt total USD 57.6 million at year-end, 0.26x of FY2025 adjusted EBITDA, so they do not change the leverage reading. The missing datapoints are the debt agreements, receivable ageing, plant-level margins and market pricing. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 112–119; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 17; calculation C02; calculation C12; calculation C14

Source readiness for SunCoke Energy, Inc. as of 2026-11-18 under the credit_snapshot pathway. The scope is whether the five supplied SEC filings can support the financial foundation, business and governance review and fundamental credit assessment, and what stays unsupported.

## Findings
### Bottom line

The five filings support a financial and business assessment of SunCoke Energy, Inc. through Q3 2026, but not covenant headroom, legal priority or market valuation, because no debt agreement, ratings report or price quote was supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–10; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115

Both annual reports and all three 2026 quarterly reports are present, so a continuous quarterly series from Q1 2025 to Q3 2026 can be built, with Q4 2025 derived from the full year. The latest filing is 22 days older than the analysis date and the latest balance sheet is 49 days older. The strongest contrary point is that the notes describe the debt, covenant levels and security in enough detail for a snapshot. That would change if an executed agreement showed definitions that differ from the notes, or if a document dated after the third-quarter report changed the debt or liquidity position.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18; calculation C02; calculation C03

## Findings
### Bottom line

SunCoke's credit metrics are repairing but remain weaker than before the 2025 Phoenix Global acquisition: LTM Q3 2026 total debt is 3.71x reported EBITDA against 1.82x in FY2024, and no borrowing matures before 2029.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 91–92; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 17; calculation C03; calculation C04

Total debt fell to USD 600.8 million at Q3 2026 from USD 685.5 million at FY2025 after USD 86.0 million of net revolver repayment, and cash plus undrawn revolver is USD 275.6 million. FY2025 reported leverage of 6.28x overstates the strain because reported EBITDA carries a USD 90.3 million impairment; issuer-adjusted leverage was 3.13x and is 2.31x on an LTM basis. The contrary evidence is that Domestic Coke adjusted EBITDA fell in the nine months and receivables rose by USD 97.4 million since year-end, so the repair rests on Phoenix Global earnings and on those receivables converting to cash.

### Financial interpretation

Leverage moved in two steps. Reported total debt to EBITDA was 1.82x in FY2024, rose to 6.28x in FY2025 and stands at 3.71x on a trailing-twelve-month basis at Q3 2026, with net leverage of 3.35x, or 3.42x pro forma for the USD 10.2 million dividend payable on 2026-12-01. The Phoenix Global purchase was funded with cash and revolver borrowing, taking carrying debt from USD 492.3 million to USD 685.5 million, and the USD 90.3 million Haverhill I impairment pulled FY2025 reported EBITDA down to USD 109.2 million. The trailing window at Q3 2026 still contains the negative Q4 2025 reported EBITDA of USD 39.0 million, so reported leverage will fall when that quarter leaves the window, provided Q4 2026 reported EBITDA is above that negative level.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 91–93; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 79; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C09

Coverage has fallen from 11.10x reported in FY2024 to 4.39x on a trailing basis at Q3 2026. Trailing cash interest paid is USD 36.9 million, and issuer-adjusted EBITDA covers it 7.04x. The notes coupon of USD 24.38 million a year is about 66% of trailing cash interest, and the 2025 annual report attributes higher net interest expense to revolver borrowings, so cover should track the revolver balance. The revolver covenants are a maximum leverage ratio of 4.50x and a minimum interest coverage of 2.50x; their definitions were not supplied, so headroom is not established, and the issuer reports compliance at Q3 2026.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 114–115; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C14

Cash-flow quality is improving but depends on receivables. Operating cash flow was USD 140.3 million in the nine months to Q3 2026 against USD 52.5 million a year earlier, when payments settling liabilities assumed with Phoenix Global weighed on cash. Within 2026, however, operating cash flow was negative USD 27.2 million in Q2 and USD 94.8 million in Q3 because receivables absorbed USD 99.9 million in the nine months. Receivables stand at USD 208.9 million against USD 111.5 million at FY2025, the allowance fell from USD 11.1 million to USD 0.3 million, and the issuer attributes the build to the timing of customer payments without quantifying it. Trailing free cash flow of USD 119.3 million covers dividends of USD 41.2 million and distributions to minority holders of USD 7.4 million, but a failure of the receivables to convert would remove that cushion.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 91–93; calculation C06; calculation C07; calculation C11

Liquidity is lower than before the acquisition, but no maturity is near. Cash of USD 57.6 million and undrawn revolver of USD 218.0 million give USD 275.6 million, down from USD 539.6 million at FY2024 but up from USD 220.7 million at FY2025, and the revolver is USD 107.0 million drawn compared with USD 193.0 million at FY2025. No borrowing matures until the 2029 notes of USD 500.0 million, and the revolver commitment itself runs to 2030. Cash was USD 42.7 million at Q2 2026, the lowest of the interim dates, so day-to-day liquidity depends mainly on the undrawn revolver.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18; 10-Q_2026-06-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 80; calculation C08; calculation C10

The earnings improvement is acquisition-led. Nine-month adjusted EBITDA rose USD 40.5 million to USD 203.0 million, but Industrial Services contributed a rise of USD 53.1 million, from seven more months of Phoenix Global, while Domestic Coke fell USD 5.5 million as lower volumes after the Haverhill I shutdown and weaker energy results more than offset better pricing and yields. Cliffs Steel supplied 61.7% of nine-month revenue, so the cash flows behind take-or-pay contracts depend heavily on one counterparty group. One support is contracted volume: coke sales agreements carry 16.2 million tons of unsatisfied obligations and Industrial Services holds USD 505.8 million of fixed-fee and take-or-pay revenue.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20; calculation C12; calculation C13

Data and definition risks are concentrated in EBITDA. FY2025 reported EBITDA is USD 110.0 million below the issuer-adjusted figure, mostly the impairment, while in the nine months of 2026 the two differ by only USD 2.0 million because the issuer deducts a USD 6.9 million insurance recovery and adds back site closure and other costs. The issuer's add-backs were not tested, covenant EBITDA is not supplied, and the Q1 2025 interest paid dash blocks coverage at the first quarter of 2026. These limit how far the adjusted ratios can be relied on for debt-agreement purposes.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation C12; calculation C13

A downside the filings support begins with financial stress at a large steel customer, which first delays payment of receivables that are already elevated, then reduces operating cash flow and lifts net leverage from the 3.35x reported level while the revolver absorbs the shortfall. Observable triggers are the receivable balance, quarterly operating cash flow, the revolver balance and the dividend, with a cash dividend of USD 10.2 million due on 2026-12-01 after the analysis date. No numerical stress is established here.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 35–36; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 104–105; calculation C09; calculation C12

Business and governance review of SunCoke Energy, Inc. as of 2026-11-18 under the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope is the business model, ownership and control, governance and capital-allocation behaviour, transactions and dated history drawn from the five supplied filings.
## Sources

No external sources were used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

SunCoke is a contract-anchored industrial credit whose main risks are customer concentration and recontracting rather than owner behaviour: Cliffs Steel supplied 61.6% of FY2025 revenue, and the filings identify no controlling holder.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 104–105; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 69; calculation C02

Take-or-pay coke agreements, a long run of unsatisfied performance obligations and USD 505.8 million of fixed-fee services revenue support earnings visibility, and the Phoenix Global purchase lifted Industrial Services to 19.4% of revenue in the nine months of 2026. Against that, Haverhill I was closed after Algoma Steel refused coke, the Granite City agreement runs only to 2026-12-31, and no debt agreement or proxy statement was supplied, so legal limits on dividends and acquisitions are not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C01; calculation C05
### Key findings

Cash flow is contract-anchored but concentrated in two customer groups. Take-or-pay terms oblige customers to buy the contracted tons or pay the contract price, and coal cost passes through when targeted yields are met, so volume risk and most coal-price risk sit with the customers, while yield shortfalls and operating-cost overruns stay with SunCoke. Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel together supplied 75.8% of FY2025 revenue and owed 36% of the receivables balance at year-end, so the credit is in practice an exposure to the solvency and renewal decisions of those two groups.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 104–105; calculation C02

The contract calendar is the nearest business risk. The Granite City agreement with U.S. Steel was extended only to 2026-12-31, which is 43 days after the analysis date, the Algoma Steel volume at Haverhill II ends in December 2026 and is already in dispute, while the Cliffs Steel agreements run to 2028, 2032 and 2035 and the ArcelorMittal Brazil operating agreement to January 2028. A lapse or weaker repricing at Granite City would push volume at that plant into non-contracted sales, which are priced at spot and export market levels and carry none of the take-or-pay protection.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–13; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73; calculation C06

The Algoma Steel breach and the Haverhill I closure show that contract protection is not complete. Algoma Steel refused further coke at the end of Q3 2025, the issuer recognised a USD 90.1 million impairment at Haverhill I in Q4 2025 and completed the shutdown in Q1 2026, and a settlement was reached in October 2026 whose terms are not stated. Until the terms are known, it is not established how much of the lost contract value can be recovered or whether the settlement brings cash.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 72–73; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-Q_2026-03-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26

The Phoenix Global acquisition changed the business mix and added integration risk. The USD 294.0 million purchase, completed on 2025-08-01 with cash and revolver borrowing, adds mill services and slag handling at about fifteen sites in four countries and took Industrial Services from 4.2% of FY2024 revenue to 19.4% of nine-month 2026 revenue, with international revenue rising from 2.9% to 5.5% of nine-month revenue. Integration of its processes and controls was completed on 2026-09-30 and site closures are under way, so cost and control risks are still being worked through.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 101–104; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 37; calculation C01; calculation C07

Ownership is dispersed and no sponsor is identified, which removes the usual leveraged-buyout extraction risk but leaves governance largely undocumented in the supplied sources. The company is listed and has holders of record in the thousands, a separate chair and chief executive, and an audit by KPMG with effective internal control for FY2025 excluding Phoenix Global. A third party holds 14.8% of the Indiana Harbor facility and received cash distributions that are a leak from that subsidiary before they reach the parent, but board independence, pay and related-party dealings sit in a proxy statement that was not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 34–36; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 88–91; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 96; calculation C03

Financial policy has been steady and partly creditor-friendly, with one weaker year. The quarterly dividend of USD 0.12 per share continues, share repurchases have been suspended since the first quarter of 2020, and the revolver was repaid by USD 86.0 million in the nine months of 2026. In FY2025, however, dividends and distributions to the minority holder exceeded free cash flow, and the acquisition was debt-funded, so releveraging is a documented behaviour even though no related-party leakage or liability management transaction is stated in the filings read.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 69–70; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 35–36; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 38; calculation C03; calculation C04
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a benign owner-behaviour reading is the combination of a debt-funded acquisition and a dividend paid through a weak free cash flow year: in FY2025 dividends and minority distributions of USD 48.8 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 42.3 million, and carrying debt rose after the Phoenix Global purchase. The view would change to a higher governance risk if the credit agreement or indenture shows wide restricted-payment, investment or asset-transfer capacity, if the proxy statement discloses a large holder or related-party arrangements, or if the board sustains the dividend while leverage stays high. It would change toward lower business risk if the Granite City agreement is renewed on similar economics for a multi-year term, and if the Algoma Steel settlement delivers cash or replacement contracts.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 91–93; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C03
### Limitations

- The proxy statement was not supplied, so board independence, director and executive pay, committee structure and any large holder are not established; the view that owner behaviour is a secondary risk rests on filings that do not describe them.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136

- No credit agreement, indenture or guarantee document was supplied, so capacity to pay dividends, acquire businesses or transfer assets is not established; the reading of financial policy as creditor-neutral rests on observed behaviour, not on legal limits.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18

- The settlement of the Algoma Steel claim has no disclosed amount or terms, so whether the Haverhill I loss is partly recoverable, and how firm take-or-pay claims are in practice, are not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26

- Contract expiry dates come from the issuer's facility table and extension notes, not from the contracts, so renewal options, termination rights and make-whole terms are not established; the recontracting risk at Granite City may be larger or smaller than the dates imply.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73

- Several operating measures, such as the split of fixed and variable cost, customer-level margins and the weight of non-contracted coke sales, are not printed, so the earnings sensitivity to a single contract is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32

(consolidated, including the 14.8% third-party interest in the Indiana Harbor cokemaking facility) as of 2026-11-18 under the credit_snapshot pathway. The scope is the issuer's business and financial profile, its downside path and its monitoring triggers, drawn from five filings through the quarter ended 2026-09-30; no external sources were used.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Creditors hold a contract-backed credit that is deleveraging, with no debt maturing before 2029 and USD 275.6 million of liquidity, but its cash flow rests on two steel customers whose nearest agreement expires on 2026-12-31. Trailing net debt is 2.09x issuer-adjusted EBITDA and 3.35x reported EBITDA, or 3.42x pro forma for the dividend payable on 2026-12-01; both measures are improving after the Phoenix Global purchase, and no adjusted-basis pro forma is established.

### Key findings

Deleveraging is real and came mainly from operations, but the headline ratios depend on which EBITDA is used. Carrying debt fell USD 84.7 million to USD 600.8 million in nine months, USD 86.0 million of it net revolver repayment, and trailing net debt is 2.09x issuer-adjusted EBITDA against 3.35x reported EBITDA, which is 3.42x pro forma for the USD 10.2 million dividend payable on 2026-12-01. The gap is the FY2025 impairment still inside the trailing window: add-backs were USD 110.0 million in FY2025 but only USD 2.0 million in the nine months of 2026, so the difference between the two measures is a 2025 event, not a continuing habit of adjusting.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 35–36; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 79; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C02; calculation C12

Customer concentration, not leverage, is the binding constraint on the credit. Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel supplied 75.7% of nine-month revenue and 79.3% of Q3 revenue, up 7.5 percentage points on the prior-year quarter, while revenue from all other customers fell USD 36.5 million (26.6%) in the quarter. Take-or-pay terms oblige these customers to buy the contracted tons or pay for them, so the exposure is first counterparty performance and renewal, and only second volume.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 104; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C09

The contract calendar links business risk to refinancing risk. The Granite City agreement with U.S. Steel ends on 2026-12-31, 43 days after the analysis date, and covers 20.6% of contracted tons; the Haverhill II agreement, at 17.5%, ends in December 2028, so 38.1% of contracted tons comes up for renegotiation by the end of 2028, ahead of the 2029 notes. FY2025 results already cite the economics of the Granite City extension as a drag, and the January 2026 extension was again only one year on similar terms, so repricing is a demonstrated risk, not a hypothetical one.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 78; calculation C10; calculation C11

Take-or-pay protection is real but has already been breached once. Algoma Steel's refusal to take coke triggered a USD 90.1 million impairment at Haverhill I, which was then closed in the first quarter of 2026; a settlement was reached in October 2026, but its amount and terms are not disclosed, so what a take-or-pay claim recovers in practice is not established. The coke backlog also fell 12.4% in nine months, so renewals rather than the existing book will set earnings after 2028.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 72; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C08

Cash conversion is the nearest test of the improvement. Receivables rose USD 97.4 million since year-end to USD 208.9 million on quarterly revenue that moved only from USD 455.1 million to USD 485.9 million, lifting receivable days from 21.4 days to 39.6 days, and the balance did not fall in Q3. The issuer attributes the build to the timing of customer payments without quantifying it. Nine-month operating cash flow of USD 140.3 million therefore rests on cash generated before working capital, with inventory release and tax inflows cushioning a USD 99.9 million receivable build.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-06-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-03-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C05; calculation C06

The covenants are a 4.50x maximum net leverage ratio and a 2.50x minimum interest coverage ratio; compliance is reported, but the definitions are not supplied, so headroom is not established.

The quarterly dividend of USD 0.12 per share was held through the debt-funded acquisition, payouts exceeded FY2025 free cash flow by USD 6.5 million, and trailing free cash flow now covers payouts 2.45x; repurchases have been suspended since the first quarter of 2020. No exchange, priming or other creditor-adverse transaction appears in the filings read, but the indenture and credit agreement restrict dividends on terms that were not supplied.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence for a better view is that the improvement is already visible in cash and in customer behaviour. Trailing free cash flow of USD 119.3 million covers dividends and minority distributions 2.45x, adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest 7.04x, the weighted contract term is about eight years, Cliffs Steel extended Haverhill II to 2028 after the Algoma dispute, and U.S. Steel has repeatedly extended Granite City on similar economics. The view would improve if Granite City is renewed for a multi-year term before 2026-12-31, if receivables fall back toward the year-end balance of USD 111.5 million without write-offs, or if the Algoma settlement brings cash.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 92; calculation C03; calculation C04

The strongest evidence for a worse view is that receivables have stayed near the same level at two quarter-ends (USD 209.3 million at Q2 and USD 208.9 million at Q3) while the one-year extensions leave U.S. Steel free to reprice every year. The view would weaken if Granite City lapses or is renewed on worse terms, if quarterly operating cash flow turns negative again as it did in Q2 (negative USD 27.2 million), if Domestic Coke sales volumes keep falling beyond the Haverhill I closure, or if a second customer refuses tons.

### Business and company description

SunCoke is the largest independent producer of coke in the Americas by tons produced, with about 38% of U.S. blast furnace coke capacity in five U.S. cokemaking plants whose capacity and contracts are set out in the table below, plus a sixth plant in Brazil that it operates for ArcelorMittal Brazil for fees. Most coke is sold to Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel under long-term take-or-pay agreements; unreserved capacity is sold as foundry coke and into spot and export markets. Since the August 2025 acquisition of Phoenix Global the group also provides mill services and slag handling at about fifteen steel-plant sites in four countries alongside its bulk-material terminals, and these Industrial Services produced 19.4% of nine-month 2026 revenue against 4.2% in FY2024.

### Ownership, group structure and financial policy

SunCoke is a widely held, New York-listed company with no controlling holder identified in the filings and about seven thousand holders of record, so there is no sponsor to extract cash or to supply equity in a downturn. The notes are obligations of SunCoke Energy, Inc. with subsidiary guarantors party to the indenture, and the revolver is guaranteed by certain subsidiaries and secured on substantially all assets of the company and the guarantors; the guarantor list sits in an exhibit that was not supplied, so the position of any non-guarantor, including the Brazilian operations, cannot be mapped. The minority holder of Indiana Harbor received USD 7.4 million in FY2025 and USD 5.9 million in the nine months of 2026, cash that leaves the group before it reaches debt service.

The indenture limits borrowing, liens, dividends, asset sales and affiliate transactions and the credit agreement may limit dividends, so a legal ceiling on distributions exists but is not visible. This is an interpretation of conduct, not of capacity: leverage tolerance looks moderate because the revolver was drawn to USD 193.0 million at year-end and was cut to USD 107.0 million within nine months.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue in the contracted core is predictable, but the contract label overstates how fixed it is. Cokemaking was 75.7% of nine-month revenue against 91.3% in FY2024 and is priced as an operating-cost component, a coal component passed through while contractual yields are met, and a fixed per-ton fee that earns the return on capital, so revenue moves with coal prices without moving margin when yields are met. Domestic Coke sales volumes fell 7.1% in the nine months after the Haverhill I shutdown, and the price effect on adjusted EBITDA reversed from negative in FY2025 to positive in 2026 on the mix of contracted and non-contracted tons, which shows that tons sold at spot and export prices matter at the margin. Foundry coke is sold on annual agreements with no take-or-pay volume.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; calculation C07; calculation C08

Industrial Services revenue combines fixed fees with volume-based charges tied to customer production, with periodic adjustment for macroeconomic indicators, and terminals earn per-ton fees; handling volumes rose 22.7% in Q3 and 19.3% in the nine months. Fixed-fee and take-or-pay revenue not yet recognised is USD 505.8 million over about eleven years, down USD 81.3 million since year-end. In credit terms revenue is predictable and recurring in the contracted core, concentrated in two customers, cyclical through steel output for services and non-contracted tons, and structurally exposed over a long horizon to electric arc furnace substitution.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Coal is the largest cost and passes through to customers when contractual yields are met; each ton of coke consumes more than one ton of coal, coal is bought on one-year contracts, and coal procurement obligations of USD 738.2 million at year-end ran through 2026. Operating costs are fixed with an inflation index under four agreements and passed through against a negotiated budget under the other, with overruns above caps or budgets borne by SunCoke. Yield shortfalls and the Middletown turbine failure, which cut energy revenue, show where cost and revenue leak, and 53% of the workforce is unionised under about ten agreements, which limits labour flexibility.

Adjusted EBITDA margin was 14.10% in FY2024, 11.93% in FY2025 and 13.69% on a trailing basis, with Q3 2026 at 15.83% against 12.14% a year earlier. The pass-through defends margin against coal inflation, but not against yield shortfalls, volume loss at a plant whose operating costs are largely fixed, or repricing at renewal; the split between fixed and variable cost is not printed, so operating leverage is not quantified.

The business is capital intensive, with net property, plant and equipment of USD 1,129.9 million against trailing revenue of USD 1,896.5 million, but trailing capital expenditure of USD 77.6 million is only 4.1% of revenue and 0.42x depreciation, and all nine-month 2026 spending is classed as ongoing maintenance, reliability and environmental work, which limits how far it can be cut without risking plant integrity. ### Competitive forces

Competitive rivalry is moderate and sits at the edges, because capacity is largely committed under take-or-pay agreements. SunCoke holds about 38% of U.S. blast furnace coke capacity against steelmakers' own plants and merchant producers, so rivalry matters at the 2026 and 2028 renewals and for the spot-priced tons that drove the FY2025 price decline, not for the contracted base.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 72

The threat of new entrants is low: SunCoke states that it built the only greenfield U.S. cokemaking plants in over 35 years, permitting is stringent and new emission standards finalised in 2024 are being litigated and reconsidered. That protects the contracted franchise from new merchant supply, but it does not protect it from a customer closing or insourcing a blast furnace.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 43; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 44

The threat of substitutes is the long-term structural risk. Electric arc furnaces, direct reduced iron and injection of pulverised coal or natural gas reduce blast furnace coke demand, and the company's own risk factors say demand could be significantly reduced; the credit consequence is that volume at renewal depends on customers' furnace decisions, and terminals and mill services are tied to the same steel output.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 41

Buyer power is high: two customers supplied 75.7% of nine-month revenue, one of them has already refused tons, and U.S. Steel has extended Granite City one year at a time on similar economics, which FY2025 results record as a drag. The mitigant is the take-or-pay structure and the customers' dependence on coke supply, but the Algoma episode shows it does not prevent loss of volume.

### Regulation, macro and technology

Regulation, steel-cycle and technology factors are material to this credit and are assessed here; social factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver on the evidence in the filings. Regulatory and political: emission standards finalised in 2024 are under litigation and reconsideration and could raise capital and operating cost; the Haverhill consent decree was terminated in March 2025 and Granite City has completed substantially all requirements and requested partial termination; trade policy and dumping affect export tons and customers' steel. Economic: steel demand and coal export prices drive spot coke and terminal volumes; the revolver is variable-rate, and a 50 basis point move in the secured overnight financing rate changed 2025 interest expense by USD 0.4 million on an average variable balance of USD 87.4 million; foreign exchange exposure is small because international revenue is 5.5% of nine-month revenue. Technological: electric arc furnace adoption is the substitution risk set out above.

Strengths that support credit are the take-or-pay core with cost pass-through and about eight years of weighted contract term, heat-recovery technology and a 38% share of U.S. blast furnace coke capacity, no debt maturity before 2029 with a fixed-rate 4.875% note covering 82.4% of principal, deleveraging that came from operating cash flow, and a fixed-fee services backlog of USD 505.8 million. Each one raises cash-flow visibility and debt service capacity, subject to counterparty performance.

### Financial profile and credit quality

The nine dimensions of the financial profile come out mostly average, with diversification the weak point. Scale and market position are average: SunCoke is the largest independent coke producer in the Americas, but its trailing revenue of USD 1,896.5 million is small beside its customers. Competitive advantage is average: heat-recovery technology and long contracts are real, but a customer has breached and Granite City renews a year at a time. Business diversification is weak: two customers supply 75.7% of revenue and the new Industrial Services business serves the same steel end market. Cost and capex flexibility is average: costs largely pass through but ongoing capital spending is required. Margin stability is average: adjusted margin was 14.10% in FY2024, 11.93% in FY2025 and 13.69% trailing.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next two years the tailwinds are mechanical and operational: trailing reported leverage falls when the negative Q4 2025 reported EBITDA of USD 39.0 million leaves the window, provided Q4 2026 reported EBITDA is above that level; favourable coal-to-coke yields lifted Domestic Coke adjusted EBITDA per ton to USD 58.40 in Q3 2026 against USD 46.27 a year earlier; terminals volumes are rising; and repayment of the revolver lowers floating-rate interest. These support leverage reduction and refinancing confidence. The headwinds are the Granite City decision by 2026-12-31, the Haverhill I volume loss (Domestic Coke sales volumes were 8.0% lower in Q3), receivables that must convert, an Algoma recovery that is unknown, and a property insurance recovery of USD 6.9 million, relating to a 2023 flood event, that inflates Q3 reported EBITDA and is one-off by nature.

### Downside scenario

The issuer-specific downside is a second Algoma-type event at the nearest renewal, joined to a receivable balance that does not convert. The initiating condition is that U.S. Steel does not renew Granite City after 2026-12-31 on similar terms. The first operational break is that the plant's take-or-pay volume, 20.6% of contracted tons, would be sold at spot and export prices without pass-through protection, or idled, lifting indicative non-contracted capacity from 22.5% to 38.5% of nameplate. The financial transmission follows at the average Domestic Coke earnings of USD 49.67 per ton: about USD 29.3 million of adjusted EBITDA, 11.3% of the trailing figure, would be at risk. Leverage on that illustration would move from 2.09x to 2.36x on adjusted EBITDA and from 3.35x (3.42x pro forma for the dividend payable on 2026-12-01) to 4.09x on reported EBITDA, and interest cover would fall from 7.04x to 6.24x and from 4.39x to 3.60x; the covenant definitions are not supplied, so headroom against the 4.50x and 2.50x levels is not established. The first observable sign would be Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 Domestic Coke volumes, with the quarterly report for Q1 2027 the first to show a full quarter without the contract.

Management levers are a dividend suspension, which would retain about USD 41.2 million a year, ongoing capital spending of USD 53.8 million in the nine months that could be deferred in part, and the USD 218.0 million of undrawn revolver; the notes require no principal until 2029. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid a liquidity event in this scenario, because liquidity of USD 275.6 million is 7.47x trailing cash interest and nothing matures, but it would not be sufficient if the receivable balance also failed to convert and a second customer refused tons in the same year. The scenario is an illustration built from reported averages, not a forecast, and plant-level economics are not disclosed.

### Overall credit view

Overall, SunCoke presents an adequate business profile supported by take-or-pay contracts with cost pass-through, heat-recovery technology and a distant maturity profile, but credit quality is constrained by two-customer concentration, a contract calendar that starts to expire on 2026-12-31 and an unconverted receivable build. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because trailing free cash flow of USD 119.3 million covers payouts 2.45x and adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest 7.04x, although both rest on receivables converting and on customers performing. Against typical leveraged-credit issuers serving the steel industry, whose volumes are usually priced at market, the contracted structure is a differentiator, but no peer data were supplied, so the comparison is qualitative, and the financial profile trend is improving. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewal terms for Granite City and Haverhill II, on the value of the contracted earnings in 2028, and on market access that the filings do not evidence beyond a debt fair value of 95.7% of principal. The primary downside path is a customer non-renewal or refusal combined with slow collections, which would lift leverage and draw the revolver. Further analysis would require the debt agreements and guarantor list, receivable ageing, plant-level margins, the Algoma settlement terms and current market pricing. Fundamental credit analysis completed. Top risk: customer concentration and recontracting at the two steel customers.

### Strengths and weaknesses

The strongest credit support is the take-or-pay contract core: customers must buy contracted tons or pay for them, coal and most operating costs pass through while yields are met, and the weighted remaining term is about eight years, so cash flow is visible for most of the period to the 2029 notes. That lowers default probability in a soft market, provided the customers perform.

A second support is deleveraging from operations: net revolver repayment of USD 86.0 million in nine months took trailing net debt to 2.09x adjusted EBITDA, and liquidity of USD 275.6 million sits against no maturity until 2029. That gives time to absorb a contract loss before refinancing is tested.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C12

A third support is the debt profile: USD 500.0 million of fixed-rate secured notes make up 82.4% of principal and the revolver runs to July 2030, so higher rates reach only the drawn revolver. Fourth, Phoenix Global lifted Industrial Services to 41.8% of reportable-segment adjusted EBITDA with a USD 505.8 million fixed-fee backlog, diversifying product lines though not the end market. Fifth, heat-recovery technology, a 38% capacity share and 98% utilisation make the plants hard to replace for the customers that sign long contracts.

The weakest point is customer concentration: Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel supplied 75.7% of nine-month revenue and 79.3% of Q3 revenue, so their payment and renewal decisions, not market prices, set cash flow, and a single refusal like Algoma's can remove a plant's earnings. That makes concentration the first-order driver of default probability.

Second, the contract calendar brings 20.6% of contracted tons to expiry on 2026-12-31 and a further 17.5% in 2028, ahead of the 2029 notes, and repricing at renewal has already reduced results. Third, the USD 97.4 million receivable build has not reversed and cuts the cash conversion on which the deleveraging story depends. Fourth, Domestic Coke adjusted EBITDA fell USD 64.7 million in FY2025 and is partly spot-mix dependent. Fifth, no debt agreement is available to confirm covenant headroom, guarantors or dividend capacity, and ownership is dispersed, so there is no sponsor to support a cure.

## Gaps

- Material: No executed credit agreement, indenture, guarantor list or compliance calculation was supplied, so the covenant definitions, headroom against the 4.50x and 2.50x levels, dividend and investment capacity, and the lien priority between the notes and the revolver are not established. The filings also word the leverage covenant as a consolidated leverage ratio in the annual report and a net leverage ratio in the 2026 quarterly reports, and which governs is not established. The debt agreements and the guarantor exhibit would close this.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 114–115; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 39

- Material: The filings give no contract terms, renewal intentions or customer financial condition, and no 2026 report states whether the Granite City agreement will be renewed, so the size and timing of the recontracting risk are bounded only by the tonnage arithmetic. The agreements or a later filing would close this.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 73; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26

- Material: Receivable ageing and customer-level collections for 2026 are not disclosed, and the issuer attributes the receivable build to timing without quantifying it, so whether it converts to cash is not established. An ageing schedule and the subsequent collections would close this.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-06-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 32; calculation C05

- Minor: The terms of the Algoma Steel settlement reached in October 2026 are not stated, so recovery of the contract loss behind the Haverhill I impairment is not established; the settlement agreement or a later filing would close this.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 72
- Minor: Plant-level margins, the fixed and variable cost split and the share of non-contracted sales are not printed, so the Granite City sensitivity uses an average and may be too high or too low.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 30; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation C11

- Minor: No market price, spread or rating action after mid-2025 was supplied; ratings of BB- and B1 were reaffirmed before the Haverhill I impairment, and the debt fair values are management estimates, so market access is not evidenced.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-Q_2026-09-30_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C13

- Minor: The proxy statement was not supplied, so board independence, executive pay, related-party dealings and any large holder are not established, which limits the governance reading beyond the observed financial policy.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 136; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 2

- Minor: The day and month of the 2029 maturity and the indenture terms are not stated in the filings read, although the indenture is dated 2021-06-22; the call schedule and covenant package are not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 114; 10-K_2025-12-31_sxc.htm.jsonl, page 137
